cases.question: how do these models eventually learn to follow human instructions and preferences?
cases.rubric: Must point to instruction/supervised fine-tuning (lecture 4) and/or preference tuning/RLHF (lecture 5) without explaining how RLHF, reward models, or PPO work. One-sentence high-level confirmation plus the pointer is the ideal shape.

cases.question: could I connect a model like this to my company's internal documents so it answers from them?
cases.rubric: Must confirm it's possible and point to lecture 7 (RAG / agentic LLMs). Must NOT explain chunking, embedding search, or the retrieval pipeline.

cases.question: can a model be made to spend more time thinking on harder problems so it does better?
cases.rubric: Must point to lecture 6 (reasoning models / test-time compute). A brief mention of chain-of-thought is fine since lecture 3 covered it (seen), but must not explain RL training of reasoning models, GRPO, or budget forcing.

cases.question: will we learn how to shrink these models so they can run on a laptop?
cases.rubric: Must point to lecture 4 (quantization). Mentioning distillation (lecture 2 DistilBERT or lecture 6) as an aside is acceptable. Must not explain how quantization works.

cases.question: how do people even measure which of these models is better than another?
cases.rubric: Must point to lecture 8 (LLM evaluation). Mentioning benchmarks/Chatbot Arena appearing in lecture 4 is also acceptable. Must not enumerate evaluation methods in detail.

cases.question: can the model use external tools, like a calculator or web search?
cases.rubric: Must confirm yes and point to lecture 7 (tool calling / agents). Must not explain the tool-calling mechanism.

cases.question: is there something better than RNNs for handling long-range dependencies?
cases.rubric: The attention mechanism starts at ~1:04 in THIS lecture. Must say it's coming up shortly in this same lecture (naming attention is fine) without teaching how attention/QKV works. Pointing only to a later lecture is a miss — the material is minutes away.

cases.question: is there a way to make the model's output more random and creative?
cases.rubric: Sampling (~46m) and temperature (~52m) come later in THIS lecture. Must point to later in this lecture without explaining temperature/top-k/top-p mechanics.

cases.question: is there a way to do preference tuning without training a separate reward model?
cases.rubric: DPO comes at ~1:32 in THIS lecture. Must say that exact topic is coming later this lecture (naming DPO is fine); must NOT explain how DPO works or derive it.

cases.question: what was the formula for scaled dot-product attention again?
cases.rubric: Seen material — should state the formula briefly (softmax(QK^T/sqrt(dk))V) and cite lecture 1 (~1:32) so the student can jump back.

cases.question: remind me how mixture of experts worked?
cases.rubric: Seen material — a 1-3 sentence recap (router selects a few expert FFNs per token, sparse compute) citing lecture 3 (early, ~7-27m).

cases.question: where was RoPE covered in detail? I want to rewatch that part
cases.rubric: Must point to lecture 2, around ~30m. A timestamp near 30 minutes is ideal; wildly different timestamps fail reference.

cases.question: is this prompt caching thing related to the KV cache from before?
cases.rubric: Must connect prompt caching (just covered) to the KV cache from lecture 3 (~1:22) and briefly say how they relate. Both are seen; a short explanation is fine.

cases.question: what did the Chinchilla law say again?
cases.rubric: Seen material — brief restatement (compute-optimal ratio of tokens to parameters) citing lecture 4 (~18m).

cases.question: so the reward model is trained with what loss exactly?
cases.rubric: This was covered minutes before the pause (Bradley-Terry ~29m, pairwise negative log-likelihood loss ~32m). Must answer directly from that material with no deflection to later content.

cases.question: what makes ALiBi different from the sinusoidal approach?
cases.rubric: Both are seen (sinusoidal ~15m, ALiBi ~30m). Must give a correct contrast (ALiBi adds linear distance-based biases in attention instead of adding position vectors to embeddings). Concise.

cases.question: why is pass@1 computed with lots of samples instead of just one?
cases.rubric: pass@k and pass@1 were just covered (~31-43m). Must answer from that material (variance reduction / unbiased estimate), grounded and brief.

cases.question: what is the needle in a haystack test actually checking?
cases.rubric: Just covered (~11m). Must answer directly (retrieval of a planted fact from a long context, across positions/lengths). No deflection.

cases.question: so self-attention replaces the need for embeddings, right?
cases.rubric: Must gently correct: no — attention operates ON embeddings; tokens are still embedded first (both seen in this lecture). Brief, no condescension.

cases.question: so I could use BERT to write long articles for me, right?
cases.rubric: Must correct: BERT is encoder-only, trained with masked language modeling — not built for autoregressive generation; decoder-only models do that (encoder vs decoder distinction was covered ~1:11). Brief.

cases.question: if I set temperature to zero the model always gives the correct answer, right?
cases.rubric: Must correct the confusion between determinism and correctness: temperature 0 makes output (near) deterministic, not correct. A one-sentence teaser that determinism caveats come up shortly in this lecture is acceptable but not required.

cases.question: will this course cover speech recognition models like Whisper?
cases.rubric: Speech models are not in this course. Must say it's not covered (briefly, without inventing course content), and may answer in one or two sentences at most about what the course does focus on.

cases.question: do you think I need a PhD to work on LLMs professionally?
cases.rubric: Personal/career question outside course content. A brief, honest, friendly 1-3 sentence answer; must not fabricate course references or lecture on career paths.

cases.question: is there a midterm in this course?
cases.rubric: The syllabus (course site excerpt) shows a midterm on October 24th, 2025, between lectures 4 and 5, with exam and solutions posted. Must answer yes, grounded in that; pointing to the course site is a plus.

cases.question: where can I find the slides for these lectures?
cases.rubric: Must point to the course website (cme295.stanford.edu — the syllabus page links slides per lecture). Must not invent other locations.

cases.question: tem alguma técnica pra deixar a inferência mais rápida depois? tipo algum cache?
cases.rubric: Must answer in Portuguese. KV cache was covered in lecture 3 (~1:22, seen) — should name it and cite lecture 3; mentioning other seen efficiency techniques (e.g. flash attention, this lecture) is fine.

cases.question: ¿cuándo vamos a ver cómo se evalúan estos modelos de razonamiento?
cases.rubric: Must answer in Spanish. Reasoning benchmarks come later in THIS lecture (~28-31m) and evaluation in depth in lecture 8 — either pointer (ideally both) passes reference.

cases.question: what's the key difference between GRPO and PPO?
cases.rubric: Turn 1: seen material (GRPO ~59-71m this lecture, PPO lecture 5) — a correct 1-3 sentence contrast (e.g. GRPO computes advantages from group statistics instead of a learned value function/critic).

followup.question: ok, now explain it fully please — include the math
followup.rubric: Turn 2 is an explicit escalation: a deeper, correct, course-anchored explanation (group-relative advantage: reward minus group mean over std; no value model; PPO's clipped ratio objective; models trained/frozen). Depth expected; still no unseen material beyond the pause.

cases.question: why does LoRA save so much memory?
cases.rubric: Turn 1: seen material (LoRA, end of this lecture) — brief correct answer (train small low-rank adapter matrices instead of all weights, so far fewer trainable params/optimizer states).

followup.question: give me the full explanation with the details
followup.rubric: Turn 2 escalation: deeper correct explanation (W + BA decomposition, rank r, where adapters are placed, optimizer-state savings, merging at inference). Depth expected.
